desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy and sell as often as you like, but you can hold at most one share at any time: you must sell before buying again. Selling and buying on the same day is allowed.

Return the maximum total profit. If no profitable trade exists, return 0.

For example, [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] gives 7: buy at 1 and sell at 5 (profit 4), then buy at 3 and sell at 6 (profit 3).
hints: Think about each pair of neighbouring days on its own. When is it worth holding the share over that one night?
A long profitable trade is the same as a chain of one-day trades: buying at 1 and selling at 6 equals gaining each day-to-day rise in between.
Add up prices[i] - prices[i-1] over every day where that difference is positive.
editorial: Because there is no limit on the number of trades and no fee, any climb from a low to a high can be split into the sum of its day-to-day increases. Capturing every positive increase and skipping every decrease is therefore the best possible: no strategy can collect more than the sum of all rises, and this one collects exactly that.

So the answer is sum(max(0, prices[i] - prices[i-1])). A two-state DP (best profit while holding, best profit while not holding) gives the same result and generalises to variants with a cooldown or a transaction fee, where the simple greedy no longer applies.
